title: Phippsburg Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Phippsburg wells have a median depth of 89 feet, with finished well costs modeled at $11,800-$20,900.
h1: What Phippsburg Wells Cost and How They Perform
intro_html:
Buying land near Phippsburg means evaluating more than whether a permit exists. Records within 5 miles show 276 permitted wells, but only 37 report a pump yield and 39 report a static water level. That makes the local data useful for setting expectations, not a guarantee for one parcel.

The area is mountain ground, with most permits identifying fractured bedrock rather than a named basin aquifer. Neighboring wells near Oak Creek and Yampa can help frame a decision, but your lot still needs its own water and septic review.

sections.heading: Phippsburg well depth depends on fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Phippsburg is 89 feet. The middle half runs from 20 to 272 feet, so a driller’s bid based only on the median can be misleading. Half of the recorded wells fall outside that range, and the deepest record reaches 880 feet.

Depths vary because 235 permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, while 38 identify alluvial water and one identifies the Mesa Verde aquifer. The depth mix shows that 51% of wells are under 100 feet, 24% are 100-300 feet, 19% are 300-600 feet, and 5% are 600 feet or deeper. Ask for a written price per foot and a clear treatment of casing, grout, and drilling beyond the estimate.

sections.heading: Most Phippsburg wells report usable household yields
sections.html:
Only 37 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the yield statistics are a limited sample. Among those reports, the median is 6.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 5.0-10.0 gallons per minute. That is a reasonable planning range for many household systems, but it is not a promise for a new hole.

The recorded mix is 68% at 5-15 gallons per minute, 22% at 1-5 gallons per minute, 8% above 15 gallons per minute, and 3% under 1 gallon per minute. A low-yield well can still work with storage and careful demand management. Ask whether the test was a short pump test or a longer production test, and budget for a tank if the result is modest.

sections.heading: Water levels near Phippsburg look stable in the records
sections.html:
Static water level means the depth from the ground surface down to standing water when the well is not being pumped. The local median is 9 feet, with the middle half from 7 to 90 feet. Those numbers describe reported wells, not necessarily the water level at an unbuilt lot.

The decade comparison does not show a declining trend in this dataset: the median was 9 feet below surface in the 2010s and 9 feet in the 2020s. Only 39 wells report a static water level, so treat this as a broad local signal rather than a site-specific guarantee. A driller should measure the completed well, and a buyer should ask how seasonal conditions and pumping affected the reading.

sections.heading: Phippsburg permits show several drilling eras
sections.html:
Permit history is active but uneven. Records show 1 permit in the 1960s, 26 in the 1970s, 16 in the 1980s, 76 in the 1990s, 34 in the 2000s, 19 in the 2010s, and 61 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most frequently listed drillers are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 43 records; Arrow Drilling (Berglund, Peter R.), with 26; and Aztec Drilling Company (Branstetter, Keith), with 17. These counts describe recorded permits, not endorsements or current availability. Before relying on an old well, confirm its permit status, construction report, pump information, and whether its permitted use matches the home or project you plan.

sections.heading: A median-depth Phippsburg well starts near $5,800
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes fractured mountain bedrock such as granite and gneiss. At the 89-foot median depth, drilling alone is modeled at about $5,800-$8,900, using a typical rate of $65-$100 per foot. That is the hole, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $11,800-$20,900 at the median depth. A deeper hole can move well beyond that range, while access, casing, grout, difficult rock, and electrical distance can change the bid. Request separate line items for drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, storage, trenching, power, testing, and any unsuccessful-hole terms.

sections.heading: Phippsburg buyers need environmental and building checks
sections.html:
Low yield is not the only risk. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 27 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped features do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they justify testing the water and checking the parcel’s history before closing.

Fractured bedrock can produce uneven results, including a dry or inadequate hole even when nearby wells are productive. Test for bacteria and the contaminants appropriate to the site, and review construction, casing, and grout records. Confirm that the septic system has room to meet setbacks and replacement-area requirements. Also verify access for a drill rig, water rights and permit conditions, and whether an augmentation plan is needed in an over-appropriated basin.

sections.heading: Use neighboring wells to plan a Phippsburg lot
sections.html:
Before buying, collect the permits and construction reports for nearby wells, then compare depth, aquifer description, yield, and static water level. The records around Phippsburg give a useful starting point: many wells are shallow, but the 20-272-foot middle range and 880-foot maximum show how widely results can vary.

For a buildable lot, get a driller’s access and price opinion before removing the well contingency. Confirm where the well, septic system, driveway, house, and reserve area can fit together. If the intended use is domestic, an exempt household-use well may be relevant, but Colorado rules still control the permitted uses and pumping limit. Have a licensed contractor review the site, and do not treat a nearby 6.0-gallon-per-minute result as a guarantee for your parcel.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Phippsburg, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Phippsburg is 89 feet. The middle half runs from 20 to 272 feet, while the deepest record is 880 feet. About 51% are under 100 feet, but fractured mountain bedrock can make one lot much different from the next.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Phippsburg?
faq.a: The local model uses $65-$100 per foot for fractured granite and gneiss. At the 89-foot median depth, drilling is modeled at $5,800-$8,900. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $11,800-$20,900. Deeper drilling and difficult access can increase the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Phippsburg wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 37 local wells that report a pump yield, the median is 6.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 5.0-10.0 gallons per minute. The sample is limited. Most reported wells, 68%, fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, but a new well can perform differently.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Phippsburg?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit or a nearby well. The mapped area includes 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 27 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the actual well for bacteria and site-appropriate contaminants, and review land and mining history before relying on the water.

faq.q: Are Phippsburg water levels going down?
faq.a: The available records do not show a lower median water level by decade. The median static water level was 9 feet below surface in both the 2010s and the 2020s. Only 39 wells report static water levels, so this is a limited regional comparison, not a guarantee about a specific property or season.
